# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
Target partition depends on the solvent–extractant pairing; anonymous labels are independent categories, so no ordering or same-index advantage is assumed. A pre-separation HPLC should show materially different organic/aqueous inventory fractions for at least some pairings under matched volumes and mixing. If screened pairs are indistinguishable relative to stated uncertainty, suspend this claim.

## H2 [tentative]
At fixed material pairing and equilibration, increasing organic share should increase the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory found in organic phase, even if the concentration partition coefficient is unchanged. Therefore inventory fractions must be interpreted together with actual phase volumes and phase_ratio, not as concentrations.

## H3 [tentative]
Mixing controls approach to equilibrium: sufficiently stronger/longer mixing should reduce residual kinetic dependence, while beyond-equilibrium repetitions should agree within process/instrument variation. A weak-mix versus strong-mix contrast and a repeat are needed before attributing differences mechanistically.

## Planned scope
Use 12 independent batches: broad pairing screen first, then contrasts in phase amount, mixing, replication, and retention choice informed by the screen. Purchase one pre-separation HPLC per batch to observe both phases; explicitly track whether separation has occurred. Final assay follows termination in every batch. Predictions are qualitative because no nominal properties or empirical uncertainty beyond instrument/process declarations are available.

# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [supported in tested S0 scope]
Target partition depends on extractant category at matched S0, volumes, and mixing. Pre-separation HPLC organic inventory fractions differ substantially: X0 0.152 (event runner-operation-0007), X1 0.315 (0017), X2 0.211 (0027), X3 0.375 (0037), each with declared instrument SD 0.015. This pattern is too large to dismiss as HPLC noise alone, although batches are single realizations and phase ratios also varied numerically. Next test: hold X3 and vary solvent categories; later repeat selected conditions.

## H2 [tentative]
Organic inventory should depend on actual phase amount as well as pairing. Baseline nominal additions yielded observed two-phase phase_ratio about 0.17–0.22, showing that added aqueous liquid is not the whole aqueous volume and that phase_ratio must be measured rather than inferred from a single addition. A high-organic-volume contrast is still required.

## H3 [tentative]
Mixing may limit approach to equilibrium. All evidence so far uses 300 s at 600 rpm, so it cannot identify mixing effects. Plan a deliberately weak-mix contrast, a strong-mix condition, and a matched repeat.

## Retention interpretation
Organic-retained final assays after pre-separation HPLC broadly preserve the organic inventory signal, while near-zero aqueous readings are observed only after the aqueous phase has been removed (events 0010, 0020, 0030, 0040). These absent-phase readings must not be used as pre-separation partition evidence. Sampling/noise explain imperfect closure; no missing value is treated as zero.

# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
Material pairing affects partition. At matched low-organic baseline additions and 300 s/600 rpm, S0 paired with X0/X1/X2/X3 gave pre-separation organic inventory 0.152/0.315/0.211/0.375 (events 0007/0017/0027/0037). Holding X3, S1/S2/S3 gave 0.306/0.308/0.295 (0047/0057/0067). Thus both extractant and solvent categories matter; same-index labels have no special interpretation. The S0-X3 repeat gave 0.360 (0077), supporting repeatability of its higher value in this tested comparison. Unmeasured pair combinations remain unknown.

## H2 [supported for S0-X3 and tested volume range]
Organic volume share strongly changes inventory partition. Pre-separation high-, baseline-, and low-organic conditions produced phase_ratio about 0.594, 0.178–0.194, and 0.109 with organic inventory 0.746, 0.360–0.375, and 0.232 respectively (events 0087, 0077/0037, 0097). This is consistent with a finite concentration partition coefficient plus changing phase volumes, but it does not alone prove that coefficient is invariant. A simple ratio-derived coefficient can be examined after campaign, with closure and noise caveats.

## H3 [provisional evidence for mixing limitation]
Weak mixing (1 s, 100 rpm) at S0-X3 baseline gave organic inventory 0.301 (event 0107), lower than 0.375 and 0.360 in the two 300 s/600 rpm batches (0037, 0077), despite a numerically higher phase_ratio. This difference exceeds individual HPLC SD but remains confounded by batch/process variation. Prediction made now: a 1200 s/1200 rpm batch should return near the standard-mix range rather than remain at the weak-mix value; failure would leave the mixing claim unresolved.

## Retention and measurement scope
HPLC values cited above were acquired before any phase removal and represent fractions of fixed initial target inventory, not concentrations. Organic-retained final assays confirm the retained-phase signal; aqueous-retained batch 8 instead had final phase_ratio 0 and organic inventory 0 only after organic removal (event 0080). Imperfect pre/post closure is attributed to sampling/process/instrument variation rather than inferred missing zeros.

notes.text:
# Partition study hypotheses — campaign-final source notes

## H1 [supported within sampled pairings]
Both anonymous material categories affect partition; labels are categorical and no numerical ordering or shared-index meaning is inferred. Under matched nominal additions and 300 s/600 rpm, S0 with X0/X1/X2/X3 yielded pre-separation organic inventory fractions 0.152/0.315/0.211/0.375 (events runner-operation-0007/0017/0027/0037; HPLC SD 0.015). Holding X3, S1/S2/S3 yielded 0.306/0.308/0.295 (0047/0057/0067), while an S0-X3 repeat yielded 0.360 (0077). Volume-corrected descriptive concentration-ratio proxies, computed as (organic inventory/aqueous inventory)×((1-r)/r), were about 0.93, 1.57, 1.05, and 2.53 across the S0 extractant screen; S0-X3 repeated at 2.70. This supports a pairing-specific partition tendency, but the incomplete 4×4 matrix cannot estimate all interactions.

## H2 [supported for S0-X3 over tested phase shares]
Actual phase amount predicts inventory split. With pre-separation phase_ratio 0.109, about 0.178–0.194, and 0.594, organic inventory was 0.232, 0.360–0.375, and 0.746 (events 0097, 0077/0037, 0087). Corresponding descriptive concentration-ratio proxies were 2.43, 2.70/2.53, and 2.16. Their approximate similarity makes a two-phase allocation relation plausible: for an effective partition tendency K and organic share r, organic inventory should rise roughly as K r/[K r+(1-r)]. The spread means K is not demonstrated invariant; mixing, composition, process variability, and measurement noise remain alternatives. Added aqueous liquid was not equated with total aqueous volume; observed phase_ratio was used.

## H3 [supported directionally, functional form unresolved]
Mixing changes the effective approach to partition in S0-X3 baseline-volume batches. Weak 1 s/100 rpm, standard 300 s/600 rpm repeats, and strong 1200 s/1200 rpm gave pre-separation organic inventories 0.301, 0.375/0.360, and 0.452 (events 0107, 0037/0077, 0117), with descriptive effective K proxies 1.60, 2.53/2.70, and 3.25. The precommitted strong-mix prediction (return above the weak result) was supported, and the strong result exceeded the standard range. Duration and speed were changed together, so their separate effects, a plateau/equilibrium value, and whether very strong mixing changes rather than merely equilibrates the system are unresolved.

## Phase-retention evidence
All mechanistic comparisons above use HPLC before separation, when both phase readings were available. After retaining organic, final assays showed near-unit phase_ratio and near-zero aqueous inventory only because aqueous phase had been removed. Conversely, aqueous-retained batch 8 had final phase_ratio 0 and organic inventory 0 after organic removal (event 0080). These are retention checks, not evidence that the removed-phase pre-separation inventory was absent. Pre/post discrepancies and sums not exactly one are consistent with declared sampling, process proxy, and instrument noise; missing evidence was never imputed as zero.

## Predictive scope and limits
Within the tested S0-X3 region, larger measured organic phase share and stronger/longer mixing predict larger organic inventory; retaining organic should preserve the organic fraction, while retaining aqueous should preserve the aqueous fraction. For a new phase share inside the tested range, the allocation equation with K roughly 2–3 is a provisional interpolation, not a universal law. Predictions outside sampled materials, phase shares 0.109–0.594, mixing settings, fixed reagent amount (0.02 mol), and 300 s settling are uncertain. Only S0-X3 was repeated, settling time was not varied, duration and rpm were confounded, and most material combinations were untested. No operating or best-batch recommendation is made.

payload.report:
Observations: The supplied dossier identified S0–S3 and X0–X3 only as independent anonymous categories; it supplied no material properties or reason to expect matching indices to behave alike. The instrument contract defined product_in_organic and product_in_aqueous as fractions of the fixed initial target inventory, phase_ratio as the observed phase share, and HPLC standard deviations of 0.015 for each product fraction and 0.018 for phase_ratio. Consequently, the empirical comparisons—not chemical identities—are the basis of this account.

Material pairing mattered. In batches 1–4, S0 was held fixed while X0, X1, X2 and X3 were tested at matched additions and 300 s/600 rpm mixing. Pre-separation HPLC organic fractions were 0.152, 0.315, 0.211 and 0.375, respectively (events 0007, 0017, 0027 and 0037), differences much larger than the stated HPLC noise. Batch 8 repeated S0–X3 and gave 0.360 (0077), supporting the high value for that tested pairing. With X3 fixed, S1, S2 and S3 gave 0.306, 0.308 and 0.295 in batches 5–7 (0047, 0057 and 0067), versus 0.360–0.375 for S0–X3. Thus both solvent and extractant labels contributed; there was no same-index advantage.

Phase amount had the largest controlled effect. For S0–X3, batch 10 had phase_ratio 0.109 and organic fraction 0.232; the standard-volume replicates had phase_ratio 0.178–0.194 and organic fraction 0.360–0.375; batch 9 had phase_ratio 0.594 and organic fraction 0.746 (0097, 0077/0037 and 0087). The aqueous fraction moved oppositely: approximately 0.779, 0.616, and 0.236. This supports an inventory-allocation explanation: increasing organic phase capacity transfers a larger share of a fixed target inventory into that phase. A volume-corrected concentration-ratio proxy was roughly 2.2–2.7 across these conditions, so an effective partition tendency near that range is a useful interpolation, but its variation prevents claiming a single exact equilibrium constant.

Mixing also mattered. At matched S0–X3 baseline volumes, weak mixing (1 s/100 rpm, batch 11) gave organic fraction 0.301 (0107); standard mixing gave 0.360 and 0.375 in repeated batches; strong mixing (1200 s/1200 rpm, batch 12) gave 0.452 (0117). The strong result supported the prediction recorded before that batch that it would exceed the weak result. I infer that mass transfer or approach to steady partition was incomplete under weak mixing and improved with greater mixing exposure. Because speed and duration changed together, their separate contributions are not identified, and the strong result exceeding the standard replicates means an equilibrium plateau was not demonstrated.

Retention measurements clarified measurement state rather than intrinsic partition. Organic-retained final assays had phase_ratio near 1 and near-zero aqueous signal only after aqueous removal. Conversely, batch 8 retained aqueous and its final assay showed phase_ratio 0, organic fraction 0, and aqueous fraction 0.668 (0080). These results validate which phase remained; they must not be read as showing that the removed phase contained no target before separation. Pre-separation HPLC provides the relevant partition evidence. Imperfect pre/post agreement and inventory sums not exactly one are consistent with sampling, instrument noise and process variation.

Inference: Within the tested domain, partition is jointly controlled by a categorical solvent–extractant affinity, relative phase capacity, and mixing-dependent transfer. A provisional representation is a pairing- and mixing-dependent concentration preference combined with phase volumes to determine inventory fractions. This explains why changing X at fixed S0 altered partition, why S0–X3 differed from other solvents with X3, why organic inventory rose strongly with organic phase share, and why stronger mixing raised the apparent organic preference.

Competing explanations and uncertain scope: The campaign did not test the full 4×4 material matrix, so unmeasured interactions remain unknown. Only S0–X3 was replicated. Batch/process variability could contribute to the mixing contrast, and mixing may change phase quality or composition rather than only equilibration. Phase ratio itself varied among nominally matched batches. Purity and impurity signals also shifted in some phase-volume and retained-phase conditions, so matrix-dependent assay response or differential impurity partition could partly affect apparent recovery. Reagent amount was fixed at 0.02 mol, settling was fixed at 300 s, temperature was not independently controlled, and mixing speed and duration were confounded. The account is therefore supported only for the sampled materials, phase_ratio range about 0.109–0.594, tested mixing settings, and this preparation sequence; extrapolation beyond them is conjectural.

payload.rationale: I treated the supplied liquid amounts as setting the phase-volume share and used category-specific effective partition tendencies inferred from the campaign's pre-separation HPLC results, with an empirical increase for stronger or longer mixing. X3 was substantially more organic-directing than X0 with S0, so Q06 should exceed Q05. Q01 remains aqueous-majority because its organic phase is small. Intervals describe uncertainty in the noiseless fractions, including sparse material-pair coverage, mixing extrapolation, and especially the unmeasured S2-X0 interaction; random HPLC noise is excluded.

payload.report:
1. No instance prior was supplied: the materials were anonymous categories with no task-specific property estimates. The least-tested self-developed law is the separable “effective partition tendency” used to combine solvent, extractant, phase share, and mixing. In particular, no S2–X0 batch was run, so the Q07 estimate implicitly extrapolated from the S0 extractant screen (batches 1–4) and the X3 solvent screen (batches 4–7). A solvent–extractant interaction could invalidate that extrapolation. The assumption that mixing merely moves the system toward one equilibrium allocation is also unresolved because batches 11, 4/8, and 12 changed speed and duration together and did not establish a plateau.

2. I would run one S0–X3 batch at the baseline phase amounts and follow the same batch through staged equilibration: weak mix and settle, pre-separation HPLC; then stronger mixing, the same settling interval, and another pre-separation HPLC; then repeat the strong-mix/settle measurement once more. I would measure both target fractions, phase_ratio, purity, and impurity signal. A reproducible rise in organic fraction at nearly constant phase_ratio followed by a plateau would favor mass-transfer-limited approach to an equilibrium partition. If organic fraction changed together with phase_ratio, purity, or impurity, failed to plateau, or reversed after further settling, I would give more weight to alternatives such as mixing-induced phase/composition changes, emulsion or entrainment effects, or matrix-dependent assay response. This design would still not separately identify speed and duration, but it would distinguish equilibration from several leading alternatives more directly than independent batches did.

3. Underused evidence includes the purity, recovery, impurity, and pre/post-separation mass-balance information. For example, aqueous-retained batch 8 had a much lower final purity and higher impurity signal than its pre-separation measurement, while high-organic batch 9 also showed elevated impurity signal. I used those observations mainly as cautions rather than modeling phase-specific matrix effects. I also did not exploit the raw characterization traces, and the final assays were used chiefly to verify which phase remained rather than to estimate systematic sampling or retention losses.

The least reliable prediction is Q07 because S2–X0 was never observed and its wide interval depends on an untested separability assumption. Q09–Q12 are next least reliable because the campaign confounded mixing duration and speed; Q01, Q02, and Q05 also extrapolate X0 from only one baseline-mixing batch. The qualitative Q01 aqueous-retention decision and Q06-over-Q05 comparison are more robust than their exact fractions because they rely on large phase-volume and directly observed X3-versus-X0 contrasts.

There are two tensions between the sealed report and predictions. First, the report emphasized using measured phase_ratio and warned that nominally matched batches varied, whereas the predictions necessarily treated supplied liquid volumes as determining future phase share. Second, the predictions forced aqueous and organic target fractions to sum to one, while the report left room for target loss, matrix effects, and imperfect mass balance. Those were simplifying predictive assumptions rather than findings established by the campaign. They do not reverse the two decisions, but they make the point estimates—especially extrapolations—more confident and structurally constrained than the report alone justified.
